subject: history
title: Judging Utility and Reliability
welcome_lead: Today you'll learn to judge how useful and reliable a source really is.
meta_desc: GCSE History source analysis — utility, reliability and how to weigh evidence.
final_note: You can now judge utility and reliability using clear criteria.

concepts.def: How useful a source is for the question asked
How trustworthy a source is as evidence
Whether the source reflects most cases or one case
Biased material aiming to shape opinion

walkthroughs.body_html:
A source is only 'useful' relative to a question.

A Nazi poster has low utility for facts about WWII battles but high utility for studying Nazi propaganda. Always ask: useful for what?

Check who made the source, when, and why. An eyewitness account is close to the event but may be one-sided.

A government report may sound neutral but hide failures. Look at content, tone and gaps. Compare with the wider context you know.

Corroboration means checking one source against others.

If three different sources from 1940 — a diary, a BBC broadcast and a German memo — all say London was bombed nightly, your confidence rises. Single sources are weaker than several agreeing.

mcqs.q: Why did William of Normandy claim the English throne in 1066?
options: He claimed Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne in 1051 and that Harold Godwinson had sworn an oath to support that claim in 1064.
William invaded because he was the strongest king in Europe and wanted more land.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.
Vesalius invented the microscope.

mcqs.q: Why was Vesalius significant in the history of medicine?
options: Vesalius invented the microscope.
Vesalius discovered the cause of disease and ended humoral theory.
His 1543 De Humani Corporis Fabrica corrected Galen's errors via human dissection and accurate illustration, founding modern anatomy though not curing disease.
The NEP was introduced by Stalin to fund the Five-Year Plans.

mcqs.q: Why did Lenin introduce the NEP in 1921?
options: The NEP was Lenin's plan to permanently switch Russia to capitalism.
The NEP was introduced by Stalin to fund the Five-Year Plans.
War Communism had collapsed the economy and provoked the Kronstadt revolt; the NEP allowed limited private trade to restore production and stabilise Bolshevik rule.
Vesalius invented the microscope.
